title: How learning can slip by even when we mean well
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton responds to an Evidence Based Education post announcing a classroom observation tool, agreeing with much of it while arguing that the lens remains fixed on teaching rather than learning. He accepts that observers rely on proxies such as busy rooms and engaged faces, and that single-observer verdicts are unreliable. He adds that learning is invisible in the moment but not over time, so pop-in visits cannot look for learning. He objects that better multi-viewpoint observation of teaching still evaluates a factor that affects learning, not learning itself. Displays, relationships and plans are all proxies, he says, and only close observation of learners tells us whether anything is sticky. The conclusion is that leaders must learn to look for learning first and only then look better at teaching.
points: Learning is invisible in the moment but visible over time, so pop-in visits serve other purposes but cannot look for learning.
Observation is weakest when it is a single, hurried, one-observer verdict; more frequent, multi-person observation with discussion produces a shared professional judgment.
Improving the observation of teaching still leaves a proxy in place, because teaching is a factor that affects learning rather than learning itself.
Displays, relationships and detailed plans can only ever be proxies for whether anything has been learned.
Teaching conversations should rest on evidence of the quality and quantity of learning first, then ask how teaching contributed.
quotes: It might surprise some people that I think learning is often invisible in the moment but this is a sentence of two halves. I don’t think that learning is invisible.
If learning might be invisible in the moment, it definitely isn’t invisible over time and over different time periods. We just need to have time to look closely.
This is not an argument against observation. It would be crazy for someone to make any comments about my classroom without ever having observed it in action.

Displays, relationships and plans can’t be anything else but proxies. When our focus is on teaching, however well we do it, we aren’t looking at learning; we aren’t looking at whether ‘anything has been learned.
We have to learn how to look, first, for learning, and only then to look better at teaching. Teaching is a factor that affects learning; it should be subsidiary to learning.
Evidence Based Education is so nearly there. But the lens they are looking through is still a lens that focuses on teaching.
